newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says moving to slower, sustainable growth.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says moving to slower, sustainable growth.

text.p: Malaysia's rocketing economic growth has begun to slow to a more sustainable rate and its worrisome balance of payments deficit is on the decline, the government said on Friday.

The Ministry of Finance said in its Economic Report for 1996/97 that gross domestic product (GDP) growth would moderate to 8.2 percent in 1996 and eight percent in 1997, following eight years of rapid expansion which peaked at 9.5 percent last year.

The current account deficit, which measures trade in both merchandise and services, would fall to an estimated 14.80 billion ringgit ($5.91 billion) in 1996 and to 11.50 billion in 1997 from 18.70 billion in 1995, the report said.
The government had earlier projected the 1996 deficit at 17 billion ringgit.

"In terms of long-term sustainability of growth, (eight percent) seems more in line with our resources," Aris Othman, deputy secretary general to the Treasury, told reporters at a briefing on the report.
The Economic Report was released just ahead of the country's national budget for 1997.
A year ago, rising inflation and growing external payment imbalances were worrying foreign investors after a similar situation in Mexico triggered an international crisis.
"This (lower growth rate) is a welcome development. Last year we were faced with the problem of overheating through price pressures, labour shortage and balance of payment deficit.
"(With) lower growth, the magnitude of these problems is now reduced," Aris said.
But problems remain; the country's employment rate was projected to fall to just 2.6 percent in 1996, amid acute labour shortages across most sectors of the economy, the report said.

Average wages rose 8.6 percent during the first seven months of 1996. But that was not matched by similar gains in productivity, which gained less than four percent in the first seven months of 1996, the report said.
A major reason growth has eased this year is falling commodity prices, particularly for palm oil of which Malaysia is the world's largest producer.
Crude oil production also declined slightly to 691,000 barrels per day (bpd) after surging to 706,000 bpd in 1995.
The torrid pace of Malaysia's building spree also abated somewhat, with construction spending expected to decline by 51 percent after growing 73 percent in 1996.
The Finance Ministry said faltering demand for electronic products in 1996 was a major contributor to slightly slower growth in the domestic manufacturing sector.
The Economic Report said real private investment growth is estimated at 7.5 percent for 1996 against 25.4 percent last year. It is expected to recover to 13.7 percent in 1997.

The pace of exports has slowed to a 4.1 percent increase in 1996 against a 20.2 percent rise in 1995. But imports are abating even more, particularly for capital goods, with an estimated rise of a mere 1.8 percent in 1996 after 24.6 percent growth in 1995.
Inflationary pressures have been largely contained, the report said. The consumer price index was projected to rise by 3.6 percent in 1996 and 3.5 percent in 1997 from 3.4 in 1995.
